# Seventh Circuit Sides with Families in Cow’s Milk Formula Cases, Reaffirms Plaintiffs’ Choice of Forum
Families whose premature babies were harmed by cow’s milk-based infant formula went to court to hold Abbott and Mead Johnson accountable. Rather than answer for that harm, the companies spent the past year litigating a different question entirely: which courthouse gets to hear the claims.

This week, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit answered them. It ruled for the families.
The companies had persuaded a lower court to move these cases out of the families’ chosen state court and into federal court, on a novel theory: that the families had not pursued one of the local defendants aggressively enough, and so had forfeited their choice of forum. It was an attempt to rewrite the rules of jurisdiction to the defendants’ advantage.
The Seventh Circuit rejected it outright. The court reaffirmed a principle that runs back to the earliest days of the Republic: plaintiffs are the masters of their own cases, and they are free to choose the forum they believe best serves justice. A defendant does not get to strip that choice away by second-guessing a family’s litigation strategy. As the court put it, if the rules governing these cases need to change, that is a task for Congress, not a favor the courts will grant powerful corporations.
The decision returns these cases toward the state court where the families first filed. And as published precedent, it safeguards that same right for countless plaintiffs to come.

## Background

Parents of children who developed necrotizing enterocolitis after being fed infant formula sued Abbott Laboratories, Mead Johnson, and Pennsylvania Hospital in state court. The defendants removed the cases to federal court, arguing that the hospital was fraudulently joined to defeat diversity jurisdiction because the plaintiffs had not actively pursued claims against it. The district court agreed, finding the plaintiffs lacked a real intent to prosecute the action against the hospital, and denied the motion to remand.

## The court’s reasoning

The Seventh Circuit reviewed the denial of the motion to remand de novo. The court noted that federal diversity jurisdiction is strictly construed and that the fraudulent joinder doctrine is narrow. The Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on July 28, 2026, in the case of Holli Carter v. Mead Johnson & Company LLC (Docket No. 25-2323), reversing a lower court's decision regarding fraudulent joinder. Each child was fed cow's milk-based formula produced by Mead Johnson or Abbott during their hospital stay, leading to serious health complications. The parents allege that the hospital failed to inform them of the risks associated with these products.

- Abbott and Mead were sued in Pennsylvania state court by five parents of premature infants who allegedly developed NEC after receiving their formulas at Pennsylvania Hospital. 1

seltz.title: Seventh Circuit Sides with Families in Cow's Milk Formula Cases, Reaffirms Plaintiffs' Choice of Forum
seltz.snippet:
Families whose premature babies were harmed by cow’s milk-based infant formula went to court to hold Abbott and Mead Johnson accountable. Rather than answer for that harm, the companies spent the past year litigating a different question entirely: which courthouse gets to hear the claims.

This week, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit answered them. It ruled for the families.

The companies had persuaded a lower court to move these cases out of the families’ chosen state court and into federal court, on a novel theory: that the families had not pursued one of the local defendants aggressively enough, and so had forfeited their choice of forum. It was an attempt to rewrite the rules of jurisdiction to the defendants’ advantage.

The Seventh Circuit rejected it outright. The court reaffirmed a principle that runs back to the earliest days of the Republic: plaintiffs are the masters of their own cases, and they are free to choose the forum they believe best serves justice. A defendant does not get to strip that choice away by second-guessing a family’s litigation strategy. As the court put it, if the rules governing these cases need to change, that is a task for Congress, not a favor the courts will grant powerful corporations.

The decision returns these cases toward the state court where the families first filed. And as published precedent, it safeguards that same right for countless plaintiffs to come.

At Keller Postman, we represent thousands of families across the country in the cow’s milk-based infant formula litigation. Decisions like this one matter because accountability begins with a family’s right to be heard. We will keep fighting to ensure manufacturers answer for the harm done to the most vulnerable infants among us, in the courtrooms these families choose.

The Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on July 28, 2026, in the case of Holli Carter v. Mead Johnson & Company LLC (Docket No. 25-2323), reversing a lower court's decision regarding fraudulent joinder. This ruling impacts several plaintiffs, including Holli Carter, who allege that their premature infants developed serious health issues after being fed cow's milk-based formula. The court's decision clarifies the standards for determining fraudulent joinder, which can significantly affect the jurisdiction of cases involving diverse parties.
The case stems from a larger group of lawsuits against Mead Johnson and Abbott Laboratories, manufacturers of infant formula products. The plaintiffs, who are parents of premature infants, claim that their children developed necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), a severe gastrointestinal disorder, after consuming these formulas. The case is part of a multidistrict litigation (MDL) proceeding in the Northern District of Illinois, where many similar cases have been consolidated.

The plaintiffs in this case include Holli Carter, Terraine Abdullah, Shondera Drayton, Gina Wieger, and Alice Stills, all of whom are parents of infants born prematurely at Pennsylvania Hospital. Each child was fed cow's milk-based formula produced by Mead Johnson or Abbott during their hospital stay, leading to serious health complications. The parents allege that the hospital failed to inform them of the risks associated with these products.

The courts of appeals have restricted fraudulent joinder to
two situations: where the plaintiff has lied about jurisdic-
tional facts, and where the plaintiff has no chance of success
against the non-diverse defendant, taking all facts and law in
the plaintiff’s favor. Consistent with other circuits’ ap-
proaches to fraudulent joinder,5 we now hold that the district
court’s view of the fraudulent joinder doctrine is not con-
sistent with the case law of the Supreme Court or of the courts
of appeals, including this court.6 Its belief that the plaintiffs
had shown insufficient intent to pursue the litigation against
Pennsylvania Hospital to judgment is not an appropriate ba-
sis upon which to predicate a determination of fraudulent
joinder. Accordingly, we reverse the decision of the district
court and remand the cases for further proceedings consistent
with this opinion.

The decision of the district court is reversed, and the case
is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opin-

ultimate.title: Holli Carter v Mead Johnson & Company LLC, 184 F.4th 608
ultimate.snippet:
- Abbott and Mead were sued in Pennsylvania state court by five parents of premature infants who allegedly developed NEC after receiving their formulas at Pennsylvania Hospital. 1
- The complaints also named Pennsylvania Hospital, destroying complete diversity unless the hospital was fraudulently joined. 2
- The cases were first removed, remanded, and returned to state court after the district court found potentially viable claims against Pennsylvania Hospital. 3
- In state court, plaintiffs conducted some discovery, and the hospital was later dismissed with prejudice on preliminary objections. 4
- After the dismissal, Abbott removed again and plaintiffs sought remand, arguing fraudulent joinder was unavailable and removal was untimely or barred by the voluntary/involuntary rule. 5
- The district court denied remand, holding that Pennsylvania Hospital was fraudulently joined because plaintiffs showed no real intent in good faith to prosecute claims against it. 6
### Issues
| Issue | Plaintiff's Argument | Defendant's Argument | Held |
|---|---|---|---|
| Can fraudulent joinder rest on lack of intent to pursue claims? 7 | Fraudulent joinder requires false jurisdictional facts or no viable claim. | No real intent to prosecute the hospital claims supports fraudulent joinder. | No; fraudulent joinder cannot rest on plaintiffs' litigation intent. 8 |
| Did the district court properly deny remand after the hospital dismissal? 9 | Pennsylvania Hospital was not fraudulently joined, so diversity was incomplete. | The hospital was a sham defendant added only to defeat diversity. | No; the remand denial was reversed and the cases were remanded. 10 |

webiq.snippet:
The district court initially rejected this and sent the case back to state court. It based its decision on a novel theory of fraudulent joinder: that the plaintiffs had demonstrated “no real intention in good faith to prosecute the action” against the hospital, pointing to their litigation conduct, such as delays in taking depositions.

Recognizing the novelty of its ruling, the district court certified the decision for an immediate interlocutory appeal to the Seventh Circuit to answer whether a plaintiff’s litigation conduct can be a basis for finding fraudulent joinder.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed the district court’s decision. It held that the doctrine of fraudulent joinder is limited to two well-established circumstances: (1) when a plaintiff makes false allegations of jurisdictional fact (such as a defendant’s state of citizenship), or (2) when there is “no chance of success” for the claim against the non-diverse defendant, with all disputed issues of fact and law resolved in the plaintiff’s favor.

The court explicitly rejected the district court’s new test, which sought to divine a plaintiff’s subjective intent by examining their litigation strategy. The panel reasoned that such an inquiry strays far from the established legal framework, improperly intrudes on the state courts’ domain, and undermines the principle that a plaintiff is the master of their complaint. Citing long-standing Supreme Court precedent, the court affirmed that a plaintiff’s motive for joining a defendant is irrelevant, provided the claim is legally colorable. The court concluded that any expansion of the fraudulent joinder doctrine to account for litigation tactics is a task for Congress, not the judiciary.  ... By rejecting the “no real intent” theory, the Seventh Circuit closes the door on a novel argument that could have been used to challenge a plaintiff’s choice of a state forum based on how actively they pursue claims against a specific defendant.
